{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=memory+experience+preference+formation+path+dependence&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"A correlational study of animation narrative style preferences, viewing behavior, and audience experience.\", \"abstract\": \"

Introduction

The association between animation narrative styles and the audience's psychological experience is a critical question in media psychology. Grounded in Uses and Gratifications (U&G), this cross-sectional correlational study examines how narrative preferences are associated with viewing experience.

Methods

Through a survey of 615 animation viewers, we evaluated how complex/non-linear, coherent/linear, and visual/expressive preferences correlate with cognitive engagement and flow experience. K-Means cluster analysis was utilized for audience segmentation.

Results

Two significant \\\"preference-experience\\\" pathways emerged: a positive correlation between a preference for complexity and cognitive engagement, and a strong correlation between a preference for coherence and flow experience. Furthermore, viewers were clustered into Analytical Viewers, Casual Plot-Followers, and Indifferent Viewers. Cognitive engagement exhibited a statistical indirect association between complexity preference and flow experience.

Discussion

These findings supply empirical evidence for understanding audience selection behaviors and offer evidence-bounded implications for content creation and platform recommendation strategies, highlighting an eudaimonic and a hedonic gratification path.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1834298\", \"pmid\": \"42936023\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13699482\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1834298\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13699482\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org…

These findings supply empirical evidence for understanding audience selection behaviors and offer evidence-bounded implications for content creation and platform recommendation strategies, highlighting an eudaimonic and a hedonic gratification path.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1834298\", \"pmid\": \"42936023\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13699482\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1834298\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13699482\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13699482?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Analysis of Opinion Evolution Based on Hegselmann-Krause Model with Historical Opinion.\", \"abstract\": \"In realistic social networks, individuals are influenced not only by current interactions, but also by recent historical opinions, prior experience, and external guidance. However, historical dependence and its decaying effect remain insufficiently studied in bounded-confidence opinion dynamics. To address this issue, this paper proposes an extended Hegselmann-Krause (HK) model in which each individual updates its opinion according to four information sources: the current opinion, historical opinions, neighbors' opinions, and a target opinion. The historical-opinion term is modeled as a weighted average of recent historical opinions, and its influence is regulated by an attenuation rate to capture memory decay over time. Simulation experiments are conducted to examine the effects of confidence thresholds, attenuation rates, weighting coefficients, and network topology on opinion evolution. The results show that low confidence thresholds tend to generate fragmented clusters, moderate thresholds facilitate opinion integration, and excessively high thresholds may lead to rapid homogenization. The attenuation rate regulates the balance between historical dependence and adaptability to new information, while different weighting configurations produce distinct evolution patterns. In addition, comparisons across ER random, WS small-world, and BA scale-free networks show that network topology significantly affects convergence speed and final opinion distributions. Finally, simulations on a real-world review-network topology derived from the Epinions dataset illustrate the applicability of the proposed model in an e-commerce-related setting. These findings extend the HK framework from a memory-aware perspective.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/e28050541\", \"pmid\": \"42187956\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13206054\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/e28050541\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13206054\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13206054?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Direct and Indirect Pathways Associated with Self-Rated Health Among Older Adults with Diabetes in China: A Path Analysis of CHARLS 2020.\", \"abstract\": \"

Objective

Using data from the fifth wave of CHARLS, this paper applies path analysis to examine the determinants and mechanisms of self-rated health among elderly diabetic patients, aiming to inform individualized clinical health management and improve patients' health and quality of life.

Method

Analyses were conducted using SPSS 27.0 and Mplus 8.3. A path analysis model was developed based on the Andersen behavioral model, and parameters were estimated with the WLSMV estimator given the categorical outcome variables.

Result

A cross-sectional study design was adopted, and the final analysis sample included 1440 elderly people diagnosed with diabetes. Among them, 835 cases (accounting for 58.0%) rated their self-health as good or average, and 605 cases (accounting for 42.0%) rated their self-health as poor. The path analytic model showed an adequate fit to the empirical data. The path coefficient indicates that the degree of pain is relatively mild (β=0.212, P<0.001), the number of comorbid chronic diseases is relatively small (β=0.400, P<0.001), there is no experience of falling (β=0.291, P=0.001), and the ability of daily activities is relatively strong (β=-0.624, P < 0.001). Elderly diabetic patients who had fewer hospitalizations in the past year (β=0.204, P<0.001), consumed alcohol (β=-0.347, P<0.001), and had longer sleep duration (β=-0.257, P<0.001) had better self-rated health conditions. Beyond their direct effects, pain, comorbidity burden, daily activity capacity, and fall history also exert indirect influences on self-rated health, mediated through three variables-hospitalization frequency, sleep duration, and alcohol consumption.

Conclusion

The health management of elderly diabetic patients should not be limited to the regulation of blood glucose indicators. Instead, a comprehensive assessment system covering physical function maintenance, symptom relief and sleep behavior intervention should be constructed to enhance patients' subjective sense of health gain in a more targeted manner.\", \"doi\": \"10.2147/ppa.s650417\", \"pmid\": \"42936735\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13702076\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.2147/PPA.S650417\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13702076\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13702076?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Temporal Quantum-like Cognition in a Free-Energy Variational Framework.\", \"abstract\": \"Free-energy-based variational principles provide a powerful framework for describing perception, inference, and decision making. The Free Energy Principle (FEP) is one prominent realization of this idea, but its standard formulation is usually expressed in terms of classical probabilistic generative models. Here, we propose an FEP-inspired, quantum-like variational approach by integrating Quantum State Over Time (QSOT), Schrödinger-bridge (SB) theory, and quantum logic into a unified framework. Cognitive evolution is formulated as the optimization of temporally extended quantum-like states under a composite action consisting of an SB-inspired path divergence, a cognitive free-energy functional, and context-dependent quantum-logical constraints with terminal target propositions. Contextual updating is modeled by time-dependent non-selective Lüders projections, while endogenous cognitive steering is represented by an internal control field. A minimal two-state toy model illustrates how these components jointly shape temporal quantum-like cognitive trajectories. The proposed framework provides a temporally extended quantum-like analogue of the variational structure underlying the FEP and suggests a general mathematical basis for modeling context-dependent cognitive dynamics.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/e28080848\", \"pmid\": \"42649643\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13512617\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/e28080848\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13512617\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13512617?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "635648166da33bc83ba5a05119b3f6115e9d7d76967feedeb6b1c6d9ce110ab6", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "memory_formed_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1834298", "doi:10.3390/e28050541", "doi:10.2147/ppa.s650417", "doi:10.3390/e28080848", "pmc:PMC13699482", "pmc:PMC13206054", "pmc:PMC13702076", "pmc:PMC13512617"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1834298", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13699482", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13699482?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3390/e28050541", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13206054", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13206054?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.2147/PPA.S650417", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13702076"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
